verdict.root_cause: An automated resource_limits change lowered the frauddetectionservice container's memory limit to 200m at 22:05:32, roughly two minutes before the earliest visible restart cycle and ~11 minutes before the alert [tr_5d90a328d546]. The JVM cannot hold its footprint under that ceiling, so the container is being terminated by the platform shortly after each bootstrap: logs show an identical JVM/OpenTelemetry-agent startup triple repeating at an almost exact ~62-second cadence through 22:17:57, with no error, exception, panic or stack trace anywhere in the window — the signature of an externally-killed process rather than an application fault [tr_ce5350e3f868]. Kafka order-consumption logging with its incrementing counter stops after 22:04:47 and never resumes, so the service is not doing useful work between kills [tr_ce5350e3f868]. The failing mechanism is the process exceeding the memory it is allowed and being killed for it — resource exhaustion — with the limit edit as the trigger, not the mechanism.
verdict.reasoning: Three independent strands line up. (1) Change: exactly one change landed on this service in the window and it is a memory-limit reduction to 200m by platform-automation, timestamped before onset, so it is a candidate cause and not a remediation; deploys, image rollouts, flag flips and application-config edits were all explicitly excluded from the change log [tr_5d90a328d546]. (2) Logs: the process is repeatedly re-executing its JVM bootstrap at ~62s intervals with zero error output and no stack traces, which the specialist correctly reads as an external kill before the application can log anything — consistent with a cgroup OOM kill and inconsistent with a hang, a single restart, or an application exception [tr_ce5350e3f868]. Order processing has ceased in parallel [tr_ce5350e3f868]. (3) Metrics contributed nothing either way: the error-ratio series is empty in both incident and baseline windows, so its emptiness is a property of the series and not an onset signal, and no container memory, limit, restart-count or OOMKilled series was returned at all [tr_152861f4d9dc][tr_d87905d7d6ea]. I therefore rely on change + log correlation rather than direct kill-reason telemetry, which is why confidence is medium rather than high. Classification: a limit lowered until the process is killed for exceeding it is resource_exhaustion, not bad_config — the wrong value is how it started, running out of memory is what is happening. The fix that actually resolves it is restoring the prior memory limit (config_revert); a restart alone would only re-enter the loop, and horizontal scaling would not help a per-container ceiling.
open_questions: No direct confirmation of OOMKill: container last-terminated-reason, restart counts, working-set bytes and the memory limit spec were all requested and returned nothing [tr_d87905d7d6ea]. The kill mechanism is inferred, not observed.

The prior memory limit is not recorded in the change log [tr_5d90a328d546], so the magnitude of the reduction — and whether 200m is merely tight or wildly below the JVM's steady-state footprint — is unknown.

The true start of the restart loop is earlier than 22:07:35; that timestamp is the boundary of the retained log block [tr_ce5350e3f868]. It has not been shown that the loop began after 22:05:32 rather than before it, which would weaken the causal link to the limit change.

Why the 22:17 alert fired at that moment is unexplained: the loop was already established well before it and no metric anchors onset [tr_ce5350e3f868][tr_d87905d7d6ea]. The alerting signal itself was never identified.

Blast radius beyond this service was not investigated — no dispatch covered Kafka consumer lag, order backlog, or downstream consumers of fraud-detection results, despite processing having stopped since ~22:04:47.

Why platform-automation issued the limit reduction (autoscaler/rightsizing policy, quota enforcement, or a bad recommendation) is unknown, and that determines whether a revert would simply be re-applied by the same automation.

proposal.expected_effect: Removing the 200m memory ceiling set at 22:05:32 should stop the ~62s restart cadence: in Loki, {service="frauddetection-service"} should show one startup triple at recreate and none for 5+ minutes after, and the 'Consumed record with orderId... total count to: N' line (last seen 22:04:47, count 2344) should resume incrementing. Container memory/restart/OOM series return no samples here, so confirm from logs, not metrics.
proposal.if_wrong: Falsified if startup triples continue at ~62s for 5+ minutes after recreate, or if they stop but consumption never resumes. Also: the change log records only 'None -> memory=200m', so if no concrete prior spec is stored the revert may be a no-op — the operator should verify one exists before executing. If platform-automation re-applies 200m within minutes, the revert is correct but non-durable and the policy must be paused.
proposal.risk: The OOM kill is inferred, never observed, and the loop's true start may predate the limit change. If the fault is in the application (leak, bad startup, Kafka issue), a higher ceiling only lengthens the death interval and hides an app fault while orders stay unprocessed. If 200m came from a quota policy, reverting may over-commit the host or cause config flap. The action is itself another container recreate.
proposal.blast_radius: frauddetectionservice only; no other service is in the given reach. Consumer-group rebalance on the order topic during recreate; downstream consumers of fraud-detection results were never investigated and may notice.

triage_judgement.reasoning: A single critical alert on frauddetectionservice with no open incidents and nothing to dismiss it as; critical severity is not something to decline before evidence exists. No signal yet distinguishes deploy, config, or resource causes.
